claims.text: A predictive approach incorporating configurational-disorder and local-atomic-environment descriptors will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity HEAs more accurately than methods based solely on average composition or bulk properties.
Configurational disorder and local atomic environments capture the dominant scattering mechanisms responsible for reduced phonon transport in HEAs.
The HEAs within scope are single-phase solid solutions with random atomic distributions and multielement compositions.
The proposed model uses local atomic environment descriptors and configurational-disorder metrics to screen HEAs.
The screening target is low phonon thermal conductivity.
The hypothesis is evaluated at room temperature.
The alloys must be single-phase solid solutions without significant secondary phases or precipitates.
Greater atomic-scale disorder and variation among local environments lead to enhanced phonon scattering.
Configurational disorder increases phonon scattering through mass fluctuations.
Configurational disorder increases phonon scattering through force-constant fluctuations.
Local-environment descriptors capture mass- and force-constant-fluctuation effects better than average-composition models.
The new approach will identify HEAs whose phonon thermal conductivity is at least 20% lower than values predicted by current average-composition models.
The new approach will correlate with experimental thermal-conductivity measurements better than current models.
Current methods rely on average composition or bulk properties.
Current methods typically underestimate the impact of local disorder on phonon transport.
The approach is not applicable to ordered alloys or alloys with large-scale phase separation.
Prediction accuracy can be benchmarked by comparing model predictions with measured phonon thermal conductivity for the same set of single-phase HEAs.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% improvement in prediction accuracy over current methods would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to identify alloys with lower measured conductivity than predicted by current models would falsify the hypothesis.
